**In Defense of Waiting**

The bus was late again this morning, which is to say it was exactly on time according to the schedule taped inside the little plastic window of the shelter, the one that has been there since before I moved to this neighborhood, but late according to my hope that it would arrive the second I got there with my coffee still hot and my coat not yet soaked through. It was raining in that sideways, indifferent way that Chicago rain does in March, the kind that finds the gap between your collar and your neck and makes a small, cold decision to live there. I stood under the shelter with a man I had seen maybe twenty times before without ever speaking to, the same man who always has a thermos and a paperback with a cracked spine, and we did what strangers at bus stops do, which is to not look at each other too directly while pretending to look at the street. The 7:15, the 7:22, the 7:30 all passed in the abstract sense of numbers, and none of them came. And for the first time in a long time, I did not immediately take my phone out of my pocket.

That sentence probably needs context, because not taking my phone out is no longer a neutral act. It feels, in public, almost like a statement. It is the modern equivalent of standing in a room and announcing that you do not own a television. People around me were already there. A woman in a navy puffy coat was scrolling with her thumb in a way that suggested she was not reading so much as fleeing. A teenager with headphones on was nodding to something only he could hear, but his eyes kept flicking up to the corner where the bus should appear, that anxious, hopeful flick. A man in a suit, tie loosened, was checking his watch, then his phone, then his watch again, as if one of them might change its mind. We all had the same problem, which was not really a problem at all. We had ten extra minutes. And ten extra minutes, in the current economy of attention, is a small emergency. It must be filled. It must be killed, as we so tellingly say. If you kill ten minutes, you get credit for surviving them.

I remember a time when waiting was not considered a problem to be solved. As a child, waiting was practically my main occupation. I waited for my mother to finish her phone calls in the kitchen, which could take an eternity during which I learned the entire geography of our linoleum floor. I waited for my father to come home from work, sitting on the curb with my bike, pumping my legs in the air. I waited for the end of the school day, for summer vacation, for my older sister to get out of the bathroom. Waiting was the texture of being small and powerless and entirely dependent on adults whose schedules were mysterious and absolute. The dentist's office on Portland Avenue had a fish tank and a stack of Highlights magazines with torn-out pages, and I could read the same three jokes for two hours and still feel, somehow, that I was being treated to an unscheduled holiday. Nothing was expected of me in a waiting room except to be quiet and to not touch anything. That seems, now, like a radical form of hospitality.

Of course, we have made waiting rooms better, which mostly means we have made them more distracting. There are screens on the walls now that show the weather, the news, our own name misspelled in cheerful letters. There is free Wi-Fi with a code you have to ask for, which gives you a little social task to complete. The chairs are better. The magazines have been replaced by charging cables. Everything has been designed, with the best intentions, to make you forget that you are, in fact, waiting for something. And perhaps that is kindness. I do not want to romanticize the discomfort of a hard plastic chair in a fluorescent room when you have a toothache. But I have been thinking lately about what we lose when we treat every gap as a defect. When a child learns that boredom is intolerable and must be immediately medicated with a screen, what does that child learn about their own inner life? That it is insufficient. That it cannot be trusted to entertain itself for even five minutes. That silence is not a room you can enter, but a noise you must cover up.

The man with the thermos finally spoke. He did not say anything profound. He said, "They rerouted the 49 last winter and never fixed it back. That's why Monday is always like this." He said it to the rain, not to me, but it was an offering. I said, "I thought it was just me." He smiled in a way that said we were both in on the same small municipal joke. We did not exchange names. We did not exchange numbers. The bus came three minutes after that, brakes sighing, and we both got on and sat on opposite sides and did not speak again. But those three minutes of shared, unfilled time had made us, briefly, a community. This happens more often than I used to think, and only when we are not sealed off from each other by our own private feeds. A waiting room, a bus stop, a line at the grocery store - these are some of the last places where strangers are still required to be in the same room with each other, doing nothing in particular, and therefore available. It is an unfashionable kind of availability, but it is real.

Airports are the cathedral of this condition. I have spent, by my rough calculation, maybe a month of my life in airports, though never all at once. Airports are designed by people who understand human impatience intimately and have decided to monetize it. There is duty-free shopping, there is a new food court that somehow serves the same four foods in a different font, there are moving walkways that do not really save you time but make you feel as though you are doing something. And yet, despite all that engineering, you still end up sitting at Gate B17 with a delay of two hours and forty minutes because of weather in Denver, and there is a moment - it always comes, about forty-five minutes in, after you have bought the overpriced coffee and checked your email and walked the entire terminal twice - when the distractions lose their power. The screen goes dark in your mind. You look out the huge window at the planes taxiing in the heat. You watch a baggage handler in a reflective vest fold a vest under his arm and drink from a bottle. You listen to the gate agent's voice, which is tired and kind and repeated, like a mantra, in a language you only half understand. Time stretches, but it also softens. You are not in control, and for once you do not have to pretend to be.

I have had a similar experience on trains, which I prefer for precisely this reason. A train, especially a long-distance train in the middle of the country, seems to be designed by romantics. You sit, you watch the landscape unspool, you cannot get off when you feel restless. Somewhere in Nebraska or Kansas, if your train is the California Zephyr, you will stop for no reason that is announced, and you will sit there in a field while a freight car passes with infinite slowness, and the conductor will say, "Folks, we're just going to be here a little while," and that "little while" might be twenty minutes or an hour. In the dining car people start talking to each other. The older couple from Ohio who are on their way to see their grandson in Reno will tell you about their garden. The college kid with the guitar will not play it, thankfully, but will tell you he is nervous about his first job. Strangers learn the shape of each other's day. When the train finally moves, it is not with a sense of having beaten time, but of having spent it. There is a difference between beating time and spending it, and I think we have forgotten the second art entirely.

We are, of course, very good at waiting when we have no choice. We wait for bread to rise, and we call that fermentation and we write essays about sourdough starters named Clint Eastwood. We wait for water to boil. We wait for the exhale of a garden in April, when everything looks dead and then, with embarrassing suddenness, everything is green and full of purpose. The farmer's market near my apartment has a stall every spring where the same man sells asparagus for about three weeks, and then he is gone, and you realize the season has moved on without consulting you. That kind of waiting is disciplined by nature, not by us. It teaches a different lesson than waiting for a bus. It says that some things cannot be rushed, and not because anyone is being inefficient, but because that is simply how growth works. A seed does not care about your deadline. A storm does not care about your flight. A body healing from surgery does not care about your calendar. We accept these waitings with a kind of grudging reverence. We do not check our phones every thirty seconds while the bread rises - or, well, some of us do, but we feel faintly ashamed of it.

The waitings that are harder are the ones that involve other people. Waiting for someone to text back. Waiting for someone to change. Waiting for someone to get better, or to get worse, or to finally die after a long illness that has reorganized the entire family around a hospital bed. Waiting for a friend to forgive you. Waiting for love to arrive or to return. These waitings have no schedule taped in a window. They are open-ended, and therefore they scare us. We try to fill them with activity, with advice, with research, with busyness that looks like care. I waited, for almost two years, for my grandmother to pass away after she stopped eating. The doctors gave us estimates that kept moving. One week they said days. The next week they said weeks. My mother and I sat in her room and read to her and played music and argued quietly about what to do with her apartment, and on the days when nothing happened, when she just slept and breathed, we felt guilty for being bored. As if boredom were a betrayal. As if we should have been performing grief continuously, at full volume. But grief, like a bus, came in waves, and in between the waves there was just quiet, and we had to learn to sit in that quiet without narrating it.

That is, I think, the core of it. We have been taught to narrate, to document, to optimize. We are living in an age of infinite commentary. When we wait, we feel an urge to announce that we are waiting. We take a photograph of the delay board. We post about it. We turn a private experience of time passing into a piece of content. This is not inherently bad - I am, after all, writing an essay about waiting, which is a form of commentary - but it changes the experience. The photograph makes the wait legible to absent others, but it makes it less legible to ourselves. We are watching ourselves wait instead of waiting. There is a moment, when I am at the bus stop and I catch myself reaching for my phone, when I can feel the old reflex rise up like a hand. I want to mooch a little dopamine. I want to know what someone I have not seen in six years had for lunch. I want to solve a crossword clue or check the weather for a place I am not going to visit. It is not that these things are terrible. It is that they are a way of leaving the room while still physically being in it. And the room - the rainy shelter, the old man with the thermos, the sounds of the street - has something to tell me, if I stay.

So I have been practicing a different kind of waiting. Not a heroic, digital-detox waiting, but a modest one. I carry a small notebook that is mostly blank. I read a book, but I leave it in my bag when I am waiting in line, because a line is short and a book is long and I do not want to interrupt a sentence for a transaction. I look at people's shoes. I notice who is wearing mismatched socks. I listen to the way the bus shelter rattles when a truck passes. I count the number of seconds between lightning and thunder when there is a storm, not to be accurate but to give my mind a task that is not a task. I think, sometimes, about nothing in particular, which is a skill I had as a child and have had to relearn as an adult with great difficulty. Thinking about nothing is not the same as thinking about what to have for dinner. It is more like watching a slow river. The thoughts come, they go, they do not need to be caught.

None of this is to say that I am patient. I am not. I am the person who gets up from the couch to check if the mail has come, even though I checked ten minutes ago and the mail carrier, as far as I know, does not run on a ten-minute cycle. I am the person who refreshes the tracking page for a package that is still three states away. I feel the same low-grade panic that everyone feels when the little loading wheel spins one time too many. But I have come to see my impatience not as a moral failing, but as a kind of information. It tells me where I am holding on too tightly. It tells me which outcomes I am trying to control. The bus, thank goodness, does not care about my feelings. It will come when it comes. It will be late on Mondays. The man with the thermos will be there, or he will not. My job is not to make the bus come faster. My job is to decide what kind of person I will be while I wait for it.

There is a temptation, when we talk about slowing down, to turn it into another product. There are apps for mindful waiting. There are retreats where you pay to sit in a room and do nothing for a weekend, which is a strange kind of nothing. I am suspicious of any practice that requires a subscription. Waiting, real waiting, is free and it is everywhere. It is in the pause before you answer a difficult question in a conversation, the pause where you could rush to fill the silence with a joke or a reassurance, but instead you let the other person finish their thought. It is in the moment after you press send on a message you are angry about, when you wait twenty minutes before you read it again. It is in the way you wait for a kettle to boil, for a song to end, for the light to change. These are tiny, unrecorded decisions to let time be time, not a resource to be mined.

Yesterday, after the bus finally came, I sat down across from the man with the thermos and he was reading his paperback. I could see the title: a western, by someone whose name I did not recognize. He was not performing reading for an audience. He was just reading, his mouth slightly open, turning pages with a thumb that had a bandage on it. I thought about how many gaps in my own day I had filled with a screen that morning before I even left the house. The news, the weather, the urgent non-urgent emails. I thought about how much of my life is spent in transit between things, and how I have treated transit as dead time, when it might be the only time that is truly mine. Not the meeting, not the task, not the performance. Just the in-between. The bus stop. The train platform. The three minutes when the man spoke to the rain. That is not dead time. That is alive time. It is the time when you are not yet where you are going, and you are no longer where you were, and for a little while you are simply here, wet socks and all, with a stranger and a schedule that does not respect you.

I do not know if I will ever be good at waiting. I suspect I will be reaching for my phone at bus stops until I am old and my eyes are bad and the phone is something else entirely. But I am trying to notice the reach, to pause in the middle of it, to put my hand back in my pocket and feel the cold seep in anyway. I am trying to remember that I waited for years to be an adult, and now that I am one, I spend an embarrassing amount of time waiting for things to be over. Perhaps the trick is not to wait less, or to wait more efficiently, but to wait more honestly. To let the wait be what it is: a brief, unscripted interlude in a day that is otherwise highly scripted. A place where time is not killed, but kept company, until the bus - or the news, or the person, or the season - finally decides to arrive, and we get on, and do not speak again, and go on our separate ways, having been, for ten minutes, exactly where we were supposed to be.
